A.explanation: Gives $4.0 \text{ W}$ because the $1.0 \text{ km}$ was not converted to $1000 \text{ m}$, so the work is 1000 times too small.

B.explanation: Work $Fx = 600 \times 1000 = 600000 \text{ J}$ divided by $150 \text{ s}$ gives $4000 \text{ W} = 4.0 \text{ kW}$.

C.explanation: Gives $90 \text{ kW}$ from multiplying $600 \times 150$, which confuses time with distance and does not calculate work.

D.explanation: Gives $90 \text{ MW}$ from a similar force-times-time error plus a power-of-ten error in the kilo to base unit conversion.

hints: Notice the distance is $1.0 \text{ km}$ while force is in $\text{N}$ and time in $\text{s}$ - convert the distance to $1000 \text{ m}$ before using it.
First connect force and distance to useful work with $W = Fx$, then connect that work to average power with $P = W/t$.
Calculate $W = 600 \times 1000$ in $\text{J}$, then divide by $150 \text{ s}$ and express the answer in $\text{kW}$ by dividing watts by $1000$.
walkthrough: Identify the useful data: driving force $F = 600 \text{ N}$, displacement in direction of force $x = 1.0 \text{ km} = 1000 \text{ m}$, time $t = 150 \text{ s}$.
State the governing physics: useful work done $W = Fx$ and average useful power $P = W/t$, so combined $P = Fx/t$.
Substitute values with units: $W = 600 \text{ N} \times 1000 \text{ m} = 600000 \text{ J}$.
Divide by time to get power: $P = 600000 \text{ J} / 150 \text{ s} = 4000 \text{ W}$.
Check units and prefix: $1000 \text{ W} = 1 \text{ kW}$, so $4000 \text{ W} = 4.0 \text{ kW}$. This is option B.
